characterization_methods.instrument_or_setup: JEOL 2010 microscope; thin foils prepared by twin-jet electropolishing in 25% nitric acid in methanol at about 20 V and −30°C
characterization_methods.key_findings: Distinguishes superdislocations of two (1/2)⟨111⟩ partials (straight, near-screw), dipole pairs (d), identical-Burgers-vector pairs (p), and straight parallel sessile ⟨100⟩ reaction dislocations (r).
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: Zone axis near [0 0 1]; imaging vectors of types 2 0 0 and 1 1 0 used (Figs. 10–13); weak-beam imaging near g:3–4g (Fig. 13)
characterization_methods.purpose: Identify dislocation Burgers vectors and examine the dislocation structures produced by deformation
characterization_methods.technique: Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) in Bright Field and Weak Beam modes, with dark field for planar (shear/thermal) faults; +g/−g imaging to identify dipoles and Burgers vectors

characterization_methods.key_findings: Smooth onset of plasticity, no discrete yield points, always slightly curved stress–strain behaviour; work hardening rate measured as the secant over the 1–1.5% strain range.
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: Room temperature, to 2–3% strain at a nominal strain rate of 3×10⁻⁴ s⁻¹
characterization_methods.purpose: Measure stress–strain behaviour and work hardening rate

defect_interactions.interaction_type: dipole pair formation and identical-Burgers-vector pairs
defect_interactions.qualitative_or_quantitative_description: Examination of the near-screw superdislocations in +g/−g conditions shows many are arranged in dipole configurations (marked d, confirmed by the change of relative dislocation position on reversing the imaging-vector sign), while other pairs share identical Burgers vectors (marked p).

defect_interactions.interaction_type: reaction of two (1/2)⟨111⟩ superdislocations producing a sessile ⟨100⟩ edge dislocation lock
defect_interactions.qualitative_or_quantitative_description: Imaging the reactions (marked r) with many g vectors confirms a reaction of two superdislocations with different ⟨111⟩ Burgers vectors lying in different {110} glide planes, producing a pair of edge dislocations with ⟨100⟩ Burgers vector in a sessile configuration on a cube plane. For example, the reaction [111] + [1̄11] formed a pair of [100] edge dislocations along the [010] direction, hence lying in a (001) plane. Such configurations constitute locks that prevent further room-temperature superdislocation motion.

interfaces.interface_notes: The two (1/2)⟨111⟩ partials constitute a perfect superdislocation for the B2 lattice but an imperfect superdislocation for the DO3 lattice, hence trail APBII faults as they glide (observed when imaging with g = (1/2)(1/2)(1/2) in B2 convention or 111 in DO3 convention). These superdislocations do not trail APBI faults (confirmed with 100-type g vector).
interfaces.slip_behavior: Dislocations are generally straight and mostly in near-screw orientations; large numbers of rather straight superdislocations of several different Burgers vectors, often oriented in near-screw directions along their {110} glide planes. Superdislocations composed of two (1/2)⟨111⟩ partials glide as individual dislocations and trail APBII faults; they do not trail any APBI faults.

comparative_performance.comparison_metric: work hardening rate (measured over 1–1.5% strain) versus Al content

service_conditions.stress_state: uniaxial compression (parallel to cylinder axis of cast samples)

processing_steps.method: standard induction melting in an alumina crucible under inert gas and drop casting into a 25 mm diameter cylindrical copper mould
processing_steps.processing_steps_notes: Produces samples with grain size of the order of 0.25 mm; binary alloy with 28% Al (atomic percent throughout the paper).

processing_steps.method: sufficiently slow cooling after solidification to develop B2/DO3 order
processing_steps.processing_steps_notes: Cooling after solidification was sufficiently slow to allow a high degree of B2 order for alloys rich in Al, and a good degree of DO3 order for alloys containing 25–30% Al (28% Al included), as indicated by strong superlattice spots and coarse DO3 domains in subsequent TEM.

Compression samples spark machined as 3 mm diameter or 5 mm × 5 mm square cross-section, height twice the diameter or width, polished on 1500 grade abrasive paper; tested to a strain of 2–3% at a nominal strain rate of 3×10⁻⁴ s⁻¹; compression axis parallel to the cylinder axis of the cast samples; smooth onset of plasticity with no discrete yield points and always slightly curved stress–strain behaviour.

measurement_conditions.other_conditions: Strained to 2–3%; smooth onset of plasticity with no discrete yield points; stress–strain behaviour always slightly curved.
measurement_conditions.specimen_geometry: 3 mm diameter or 5 mm × 5 mm square cross-section, height twice the diameter or width; compression axis parallel to the cylinder axis of the cast samples

defects.type: superdislocations composed of two (1/2)⟨111⟩ partials (near-screw, generally straight); edge dipole segments and dipole loops; identical-Burgers-vector dislocation pairs; sessile ⟨100⟩ edge dislocations from reactions between superdislocations

phases_present.crystal_structure: ordered bcc — B2 ordered, with a good degree of DO3 order (25–30% Al range)
phases_present.phase_name: Fe–28% Al ordered matrix (B2 order with additional DO3 order)

microstructure_list.region: centre of the deformed sample (TEM foils cut perpendicular to the stress axis from the centre of deformed samples)

structures.overall_structure: Deformed (2–3% strain) Fe–28% Al in which dislocations are invariably superdislocations composed of two (1/2)⟨111⟩ partials (perfect superdislocation for the B2 lattice but imperfect for the DO3 lattice), generally straight and mostly in near-screw orientations, with many dipole configurations, identical-Burgers-vector pairs and reaction products giving sessile ⟨100⟩ edge dislocations.

unmapped_findings: The work hardening rate peak of the Fe–28% Al alloy coincides with a strong peak in the elastic anisotropy (Zener factor A reaching between 6 and 7 around 28–30% Al); the peak is attributed to high Peierls forces (core effects) rather than to the elastic anisotropy itself.

The small ductility maximum of Fe–28% Al (~5–6%) is explained by the Considère criterion as arising from the high work hardening rate over the 26–30% Al range where the flow stress is relatively constant.

No APB tubes were observed in the Fe–28% Al alloy; the higher work hardening of the ordered state is attributed to the formation of superdislocation dipole locks and the increased tendency of dislocations to lie in screw orientations.

For the Fe–28% Al alloy, reaction of different ⟨111⟩ superdislocations to produce straight sessile ⟨100⟩ edge dislocations (Peierls forces extremely high at room temperature) creates strong barriers to further glide of ⟨111⟩ superdislocations, potentially contributing to the high work hardening.
